stem: Trap counts fall after treatment, but half the traps were removed at the same time. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Treat the apparent decline as confounded because trap density changed; normalize to comparable effort or collect a matched follow-up before attributing improvement.
Credit the intervention with a 50% reduction because total catch remained lower after half the traps were removed.
Count removed traps as zero-catch observations so the post-treatment denominator remains comparable with the original round.
Discard the earlier round and use only the reduced-trap layout because it reflects the current scouting configuration.
rationale: Changing the number of traps changes sampling effort, so raw counts before and after removal are not directly comparable. A lower total catch may simply reflect fewer opportunities to detect the pest. The defensible interpretation is to account for effort or collect a comparable follow-up before claiming improvement. Treating removed traps as zero or discarding the earlier round manufactures comparability rather than preserving the actual sampling change.
